questions.stem: Arteries have thick muscular walls and a small lumen. How do these features relate to their function?

options.text: Thick walls slow blood flow; small lumen stores more blood
Thick walls withstand high blood pressure from the heart; the small lumen helps maintain high pressure
Thick walls absorb nutrients; small lumen prevents blood clotting
Thick walls insulate the blood; small lumen increases blood volume

questions.explanation: Arteries carry blood away from the heart at high pressure. Their thick walls (with muscle and elastic tissue) withstand and smooth out the surges of high pressure from each heartbeat. The relatively narrow lumen helps maintain this high pressure. The elastic tissue stretches and recoils with each pulse, smoothing blood flow.

questions.stem: Capillaries have walls that are only one cell thick. Why is this essential for their function?

options.text: Thin walls allow capillaries to stretch to accommodate more blood
Thin walls provide a short diffusion distance for efficient exchange of substances (oxygen, glucose, CO2) between blood and tissues
Thin walls make capillaries invisible under a microscope
Thin walls allow capillaries to contract and push blood forward

questions.explanation: Capillaries are the site of substance exchange between blood and body tissues. Their walls being only one cell thick means the diffusion distance is minimal, allowing oxygen, glucose, and other nutrients to diffuse quickly from the blood to the cells, and waste products (CO2, urea) to diffuse from cells back into the blood.

questions.stem: Veins have valves but arteries generally do not. Why do veins need valves?

options.text: Veins carry blood at high pressure, so valves prevent vessel damage
Veins carry blood at low pressure, so valves prevent blood from flowing backwards, especially against gravity
Valves help veins pump blood like the heart
Valves filter out waste products in venous blood

questions.explanation: Blood in veins is at low pressure (having lost pressure passing through capillary beds). Without valves, blood would pool in the lower body due to gravity. Valves ensure one-way flow back toward the heart. Arteries do not need valves because the high pressure from the heart keeps blood moving forward. Skeletal muscle contractions also help squeeze blood through veins.

questions.stem: A nurse takes a blood sample from a vein in the arm rather than an artery. Why are veins preferred for blood sampling?

options.text: Veins contain more blood than arteries
Veins are closer to the surface, have thinner walls, and are at lower pressure, making them safer and easier to access
Venous blood contains more information than arterial blood
Arteries do not contain enough blood for testing

questions.explanation: Veins are more superficial (closer to the skin surface), have thinner walls that are easier to puncture, and carry blood at much lower pressure. If an artery were punctured, the high pressure would cause rapid, dangerous bleeding that is difficult to stop. Venous blood can be used for most diagnostic tests.

questions.stem: A student is given cross-sections of three blood vessels to identify. Vessel A has a thick wall with lots of muscle and elastic tissue. Vessel B has a very thin wall, one cell thick. Vessel C has a thin wall with valves and a large lumen. Identify the vessels.

options.text: A = vein, B = artery, C = capillary
A = capillary, B = vein, C = artery
A = artery, B = capillary, C = vein
A = artery, B = vein, C = capillary

questions.explanation: Vessel A (thick muscular/elastic wall) = artery, designed to withstand high pressure. Vessel B (one cell thick wall) = capillary, for efficient substance exchange. Vessel C (thin wall, valves, large lumen) = vein, carrying blood at low pressure back to the heart. These structural differences directly relate to each vessel's function.
